title: America’s Next Top Paddy’s Billboard Model Contest

jokes.text: Who spent $500 for laser hair removal?
jokes.setup: Frank is reading off absurd company credit card charges one by one
jokes.punchline: The first charge is laser hair removal — immediately signals the escalating ridiculousness to come
jokes.explanation: The joke works as the first beat in a list-escalation structure. Functional but not special on its own — it's the setup for the whole sequence.

jokes.text: Right over here, slick. Don't want to have hair down there. You know what I'm saying?
jokes.setup: Frank asks who spent $500 on laser hair removal, expecting embarrassment
jokes.punchline: Mac owns it completely with smug confidence and zero shame, calling Frank 'slick'
jokes.explanation: Mac's total lack of self-awareness is perfectly in character. The 'you know what I'm saying?' is a nice touch — he genuinely thinks this is relatable. Good character-specific comedy.

jokes.text: Who spent $5,000 for a samurai sword? / Your head of security. / Yeah. Just wait till he saves your life one day with it.
jokes.setup: Frank escalates the credit card charges; a samurai sword is an absurd security expense
jokes.punchline: Mac has appointed a 'head of security' armed with a samurai sword, delivered with total earnestness about its utility
jokes.explanation: The 'head of security' framing is a great Mac detail — it implies a whole off-screen institutional hierarchy he's invented. 'Just wait till he saves your life one day' is a confident absurdist promise that lands well.

jokes.text: I'm going to take all those hilarious characters I've been creating over the past several years, put them on tape, put them on YouTube. That way I can get discovered by a casting director or producer, get some kind of a TV development deal.
jokes.setup: Frank asks about a $6,000 camcorder charge
jokes.punchline: Dee's explanation reveals a delusional multi-step career plan that is painfully naive and self-aggrandizing
jokes.explanation: Classic Dee delusion — the specificity of 'TV development deal' makes it funnier than a vague acting dream. Character integration is high because this is Dee's core tragic flaw. Slightly bloated delivery hurts economy.

jokes.text: Yeah, right. So the point is, Frank, is that these are all business expenses. I mean, some are definitely more realistic than others. - Yeah. Not that one. - No, not at all.
jokes.setup: Dennis defends all the charges as business expenses
jokes.punchline: He and Mac immediately agree that Dee's YouTube plan is not realistic — the brief conspiratorial aside is the gag
jokes.explanation: The quick conspiratorial agreement between Dennis and Mac at Dee's expense is a solid beat. Economy is good — it's two lines. But it's a fairly standard 'gang dismisses Dee' joke.

jokes.text: It is really astonishing how bad your idea is.
jokes.setup: Charlie pitches his billboard idea: a Green Man kicking someone in the nuts with drink specials
jokes.punchline: Dennis's response is delivered with the calm certainty of someone explaining gravity — not angry, just genuinely stunned
jokes.explanation: Perfect economy — the word 'astonishing' elevates a simple dismissal into something specific. The deadpan delivery implied by the writing is very Dennis. One of the more quotable putdowns in the episode.

jokes.text: Go sit down. The adults are working. The adults are working. When we need a child, we'll call you.
jokes.setup: Charlie protests Dennis's dismissal of his billboard idea
jokes.punchline: Mac, who is himself deeply childish and useless, dismisses Charlie as a child and tells him the 'adults' are working — the irony being that Mac is no more of an adult
jokes.explanation: The repetition of 'The adults are working' adds a pompous rhythm. The irony of Mac positioning himself as an adult is implicit but effective.

jokes.text: It's Advertising 101: long legs, taut breasts and tight poopers.
jokes.setup: Mac and Dennis agree sex sells on a billboard; Mac begins listing conventionally sexy features
jokes.punchline: The list ends with 'tight poopers' — a jarring anatomical vulgarity that reveals Mac's specific and unfiltered inner monologue
jokes.explanation: One of the best lines in the episode. The setup of 'long legs, taut breasts' is a cliché advertising list — the word 'poopers' is simultaneously childish and specific in a way that feels distinctly Mac. The 'Advertising 101' framing as fake wisdom is perfect character comedy. High quotability because it's unexpected and oddly clinical.

jokes.text: Dee preemptively narrates her own humiliation: 'I would volunteer to be the girl on the billboard, and then you guys would talk about how ugly you think I am, and compare me to some sort of giant bird.'
jokes.setup: The gang is discussing who to put on the billboard
jokes.punchline: Dee breaks the fourth wall of their social dynamic by scripting the exact insult she knows is coming — but they still deliver it anyway
jokes.explanation: Smart, layered writing. Dee calling out the pattern ahead of time is a meta-commentary on the show's own running gag, and the fact that Dennis and Mac STILL can't help themselves ('You look so much like a bird,' 'fish recently') makes it land harder. The escalation to 'fish' shows they're not even using the same insult — their cruelty is organic, not scripted. Strong character integration.

jokes.text: You look so much like a bird. / Dennis, I was thinking fish recently. / Yeah. Her eyes are so far apart, they're like they're on...
jokes.setup: Dee just predicted they'd compare her to a giant bird
jokes.punchline: They immediately confirm it, then escalate to 'fish' — the disagreement about WHICH animal she resembles is a bonus joke within the insult
jokes.explanation: The pivot from bird to fish — with the implication that her eyes are so wide-set they're on the sides of her head — is a creative escalation. Works in tandem with joke #8 as a callback payoff.

jokes.text: "S" you in your "A"s, don't wear "C"s, and "J" all over your "B"s.
jokes.setup: Charlie is leaving and says a cheerful goodbye
jokes.punchline: His acronym farewell is a coded extremely vulgar phrase delivered with total innocent cheerfulness — the audience has to decode it
jokes.explanation: One of the best jokes in the episode. The letter-substitution creates a satisfying puzzle for the audience that resolves into something shockingly graphic ('See you in your ass, don't wear condoms, and jizz all over your boobs'). Charlie's breezy delivery — as if this is a totally normal farewell — is essential. High quotability because it's memorable, repeatable, and just obscure enough to feel like a secret. The follow-up reaction ('Why would he not want a C...?') is a perfect button.

jokes.text: Why would he not want a "C"...? / I don't even know what he's talking about half the time, bro.
jokes.setup: Charlie exits with the coded vulgar farewell
jokes.punchline: Mac starts to decode it, gets stuck on the condom part as if that's the confusing element — Dennis's weary resignation is the button
jokes.explanation: Perfect button on the previous joke. Mac focusing on the C (condoms) rather than the more shocking elements, and Dennis's resigned 'half the time' — implying this is routine — is a great two-line payoff. Economy is excellent.

jokes.text: two gorgeous girls up there, giant cans, me in the middle with my thumbs up.
jokes.setup: Frank confidently announces he already knows what the billboard will look like
jokes.punchline: His vision places himself — an older, unattractive man — flanked by hot women giving a thumbs up, as if this is an obviously correct billboard
jokes.explanation: Classic Frank delusion. The 'thumbs up' detail is a good specific touch — not just a wink or a smile, but the most generic form of approval. Functional character comedy.

jokes.text: You're... ugly. / What? Ugly? / With that anteater nose, you're telling me I'm ugly?
jokes.setup: Mac and Dennis discuss whether Frank could be the face of the bar
jokes.punchline: Mac bluntly calls Frank ugly; Frank deflects by attacking Mac's nose, calling it an 'anteater nose'
jokes.explanation: 'Anteater nose' is a good specific insult — not generic. The structure of the deflection (accuse the accuser) is predictable but executed with appropriate energy. Solid but unremarkable.

jokes.text: My nose was chiseled by the gods themselves, Frank. My body was sculpted to the proportions of Michelangelo's David.
jokes.setup: Frank and Mac are insulting each other's looks; Dennis intervenes
jokes.punchline: Dennis defends his own appearance with grandiose mythological language — revealing his messiah-level narcissism
jokes.explanation: Peak Dennis. 'Chiseled by the gods themselves' is the exact level of self-mythology Dennis operates at. The Michelangelo's David reference adds classical weight to his vanity. This is one of the lines that most clearly defines his character — high character integration. Quotable.

jokes.text: You, on the other hand, well... you're a pit of despair. Frank, you disgust me. You disgust everyone. And you will never, ever be on that billboard.
jokes.setup: Dennis has just finished praising his own body; he pivots to Frank
jokes.punchline: 'Pit of despair' is a bizarrely poetic insult, followed by the escalating 'you disgust everyone' (not just me, everyone) — the finality of 'never, ever' is hilariously dramatic
jokes.explanation: 'Pit of despair' is a genuinely unexpected phrase — it has a literary quality that makes it funnier than a standard insult. The escalation from 'me' to 'everyone' is a nice structural beat. Dennis's confident authority over Frank's self-worth is good character work.

jokes.text: Good morning, Philadelphia! I'm Crazy Paddy, and I'm coming to you from Paddy's Pub...
jokes.setup: Dee is filming her 'viral video' character — a wacky local TV ad mascot called 'Crazy Paddy'
jokes.punchline: The character is exactly what Charlie described it as: a bad late-night cable commercial, performed with total sincerity by Dee
jokes.explanation: The humor is Dee's obliviousness. The character itself isn't funny — which is the point — but the joke lands mostly in the reaction, not the content. Functions as setup for the YouTube-hitting sequence.

jokes.text: No. That's not what YouTube videos are like. That's like a bad late-night commercial you'd see on the cable network or something.
jokes.setup: Dee finishes performing 'Crazy Paddy' and asks if Charlie liked it
jokes.punchline: Charlie's accurate diagnosis — it's just a bad cable commercial — is funnier because he's about to replace it with something equally terrible
jokes.explanation: Charlie is correct, which is funny, but his authority here is ironic since his alternative (volleyballs to the face) is no better. Good setup for the escalation.

jokes.text: Maybe you didn't get it. I'm crazy 'cause I'm pricing the beer too low.
jokes.setup: Charlie says Crazy Paddy is a bad idea
jokes.punchline: Dee's explanation reveals she thinks the concept needs explaining — the idea that pricing beer too low = crazy is so thin it's funny that she's proud of it
jokes.explanation: The irony of Dee explaining her joke only makes it worse — a classic comedy trap. Her earnestness is the joke. Good character-specific moment.

jokes.text: Charlie suddenly launches a volleyball directly into Dee's face mid-performance, completely unexpected.
jokes.setup: Dee is about to restart 'Crazy Paddy'; Charlie says he has a better idea for YouTube content
jokes.punchline: Without warning, a volleyball smashes Dee in the face — Charlie's idea of viral content is literal physical assault
jokes.explanation: The physical gag works because it's sudden and because Charlie's logic ('People getting injured or seriously hurt — that's funny!') is both wrong and weirdly correct about YouTube. The commitment to the bit — repeated face shots — escalates it well. Economy is high: no buildup, just impact.

jokes.text: You ever see those girls mashing the grapes, and then slips and she's, like...? That's what YouTube video is. People getting injured or seriously hurt — that's funny!
jokes.setup: Dee is upset about being hit with a volleyball
jokes.punchline: Charlie's reference to the famous 'grape lady' viral video — and his earnest endorsement of injury as comedy — is delivered as a media theory lesson
jokes.explanation: The grape-stomping reference is a sharp 2008 cultural touchpoint. Charlie's sincere media analysis is funny because it's not entirely wrong. Good character voice.

jokes.text: I'll blast you all over if you flinch again.
jokes.setup: Dee keeps flinching because she knows the volleyball is coming
jokes.punchline: Charlie's threat — which is both about volleyballs and unintentionally sexual/violent — is delivered with complete earnestness
jokes.explanation: The double meaning is accidental on Charlie's part, which is what makes it funny. Good economy — the line does double duty without trying.

jokes.text: It doesn't hurt too bad.
jokes.setup: Dee has been hit in the face repeatedly with a volleyball; there's a pause after the last hit
jokes.punchline: Dee's understatement — delivered presumably with a swollen, red face — is a perfect example of resigned suffering
jokes.explanation: The humor is entirely in the visual context implied (face hit multiple times) versus the mild statement. Perfect economy — four words do all the work. The beaten-down Dee is a recurring pleasure.

jokes.text: Bro, can you believe how many hot chicks showed up for a casting call for a billboard? How have we not done this before?
jokes.setup: Mac and Dennis are running a billboard model casting call
jokes.punchline: Mac's reflection implies this is primarily a scheme to meet women, and his genuine amazement that it works is the joke
jokes.explanation: Functional scene-transition joke. Mac's obliviousness to his own motives is classic, though this reads as a relatively soft beat.

jokes.text: Dennis Reynolds, 40 feet tall and shirtless. It's going to be so perfect!
jokes.setup: Dennis and Mac are excited about the casting call
jokes.punchline: Dennis has mentally already won and is visualizing the specific dimensions of his own image — the 'so perfect!' is delirious with self-admiration
jokes.explanation: Good Dennis narcissism. '40 feet tall' is a funny specific detail — he's thought about the dimensions. The 'so perfect!' is appropriately unhinged.

jokes.text: I went on a stud hunt. I came back with beefcake.
jokes.setup: Frank appears with a group of large, muscular men
jokes.punchline: Frank's self-satisfied summary of his activity — 'stud hunt' as a legitimate errand — is delivered with complete pride
jokes.explanation: Excellent economy — two short sentences that paint a complete absurd picture. 'Stud hunt' as an activity that Frank clearly executed with military focus is very funny. Good Frank character voice.

jokes.text: Rex? Rex? / What are these guys for? We don't need Rex. / Take your shirt off.
jokes.setup: Dennis protests that he's the male model and they don't need Rex
jokes.punchline: Frank immediately orders Rex to take his shirt off — bypassing Dennis's objection entirely
jokes.explanation: The joke is in Frank's complete disregard for Dennis's feelings. The structure — protest immediately overridden by action — is clean and efficient. 'Rex' as a name is inherently funny for a human male model.

jokes.text: Now, that, that is what you call a stallion. That is a stallion. / I didn't know you were looking for a stallion. I'm a stallion.
jokes.setup: Rex takes his shirt off; Mac is visibly moved
jokes.punchline: Mac and Frank declare Rex a 'stallion'; Dennis insists he's also a stallion — the word becomes absurd through repetition, and Dennis's self-insertion is desperate
jokes.explanation: The repetition of 'stallion' builds absurdly, and Dennis's claim to the same title while being clearly outclassed is classic Dennis denial. Mac's enthusiasm for Rex has undercurrents the show doesn't address directly, adding a layer.

jokes.text: All right, this is messy. Look, buddy, 2003 Dennis, okay, he was Grade-A prime beefcake. No one is disputing that. He was a stallion. But 2008 Dennis is in decline.
jokes.setup: Dennis insists he can compete with Rex as a model
jokes.punchline: Mac delivers a measured, almost sympathetic career retrospective on Dennis's body, using year-specific labels and financial terminology ('Grade-A prime') as if assessing livestock
jokes.explanation: Excellent writing. The year-stamping ('2003 Dennis,' '2008 Dennis') treats Dennis as a commodity product with a shelf life. 'Grade-A prime' applies meat-grading to a person. The sympathy in Mac's delivery — 'No one is disputing that' — makes it funnier and crueler. This would be a standout line in any episode.

jokes.text: I bet if you pop those pants off, you're gonna find a bird that just won't quit either. And I think that'll come in handy in this situation. I think the problem here is that your body quit. Your bird quit. And unfortunately, it's no longer legit.
jokes.setup: Mac describes Rex's 'body that just won't quit'
jokes.punchline: Frank extrapolates to Rex's genitals ('bird'), then delivers an accidental rhyme scheme — 'quit/legit' — as an unplanned dismissal of Dennis that also scans as poetry
jokes.explanation: The accidental rhyme ('quit/legit') elevates what would be a simple crude joke into something unexpectedly structured. Frank's confident assessment of Rex's genitalia and simultaneous dismissal of Dennis's is very Frank. The beat is a bit long but lands.

jokes.text: Attention, ladies, I'm gonna need all the A cups to please head for the back door.
jokes.setup: Mac is running the female model auditions
jokes.punchline: His opening announcement immediately disqualifies a portion of women based on bra size — the casual cruelty delivered in professional audition language is jarring
jokes.explanation: The professional tone ('Attention, ladies') contrasted with the crude disqualification is good. 'Head for the back door' has an unintentional/intentional double meaning. Good economy.

jokes.text: Her name's Martina Martinez, and she is a streetwise Puerto Rican girl who's always quick with a sassy comeback.
jokes.setup: Charlie asks who Dee's character is
jokes.punchline: Dee describes 'Martina Martinez' — a broad ethnic stereotype she's about to perform with complete conviction — the description alone signals the cringe
jokes.explanation: The joke is about Dee's oblivious racism masquerading as comedic range. The name 'Martina Martinez' is comically unimaginative. This is cringe comedy — the audience's discomfort IS the joke. The setup works better than the execution.

jokes.text: You were brought here because you are the most beautiful people in all of Philadelphia. And as such, the honor has been bestowed upon all of you to compete in Paddy's first Next Top Billboard Model contest.
jokes.setup: Mac addresses the assembled models
jokes.punchline: The grandiosity of 'the honor has been bestowed upon all of you' for a local bar's unpaid billboard is comically inflated — Mac genuinely believes this is prestigious
jokes.explanation: Good illustration of Mac's grandiosity applied to something trivial. The 'honor has been bestowed' construction is nicely pompous. Functional but not exceptional.

jokes.text: What's the pay? / The pay, sir, is getting your face 40 feet up on a billboard. / So there's no pay then? / I just told you what the pay was.
jokes.setup: Mac finishes his grand speech about the honor of competing
jokes.punchline: An immediate flat challenge — 'what's the pay?' — deflates the whole thing; Mac's insistence that exposure IS pay is a perfect lampoon of creative industry exploitation
jokes.explanation: The 'exposure as pay' joke has aged perfectly — it's a timeless comment on unpaid creative work. The structure is clean: idealism → reality check → denial → walkout. 'He told you what the goddamn pay was' from Frank adds a great button. Very economical.

jokes.text: Let's take their lack of dedication as a lesson, shall we? Competitions like this aren't about money. They're about fame.
jokes.setup: Multiple people leave after learning there's no pay
jokes.punchline: Mac reframes mass walkouts as a 'lesson' in dedication — his ability to spin humiliation into inspiration is delusional and funny
jokes.explanation: Mac's inspirational speech in the face of obvious failure is good character work. 'Lack of dedication' reframing rational economic behavior as a moral failing is the kind of motivated reasoning the gang always employs.

jokes.text: Dennis shows up wanting to enter the competition after being excluded. / Judges' sidebar. / Do you want to let him in? / Bro, he's been talking about this modeling thing for years. If only to shut him up.
jokes.setup: Dennis dramatically approaches the competition he was excluded from
jokes.punchline: The 'judges' sidebar' is a comically formal procedure for two people; and Mac's reason for including Dennis — 'if only to shut him up' — is an honest admission of exhaustion with Dennis
jokes.explanation: 'If only to shut him up' is a genuinely honest friendship moment wrapped in cruelty. The 'judges' sidebar' formal language for a two-person whisper is good structural comedy.

jokes.text: Oh, yeah! Yes! Huh?
jokes.setup: Frank and Mac let Dennis into the competition
jokes.punchline: Dennis's victory celebration — 'Oh yeah! Yes! Huh?' — is disproportionately triumphant for being allowed into an unpaid local bar contest
jokes.explanation: The gap between Dennis's reaction and the actual achievement is the joke. The 'Huh?' at the end — a flex at no one in particular — is a funny specific detail. Visual comedy implied by the exaggerated celebration.

jokes.text: Okay, the first competion is the underwear competion.
jokes.setup: Mac announces the first event of the model competition
jokes.punchline: Without any transition or justification, the first event is simply 'the underwear competition' — Mac sees no need to explain why this is relevant to a billboard
jokes.explanation: The abruptness is the joke. Mac just decides the first event involves men in underwear with no justification. This feeds into the show's ongoing ambiguity about Mac's sexuality.

jokes.text: Boom! (Dennis's reaction to the underwear competition announcement, presumably striking a pose)
jokes.setup: Mac announces the underwear competition
jokes.punchline: Dennis's immediate 'Boom!' suggests he's already posing — the word functions as a self-satisfied sound effect for his own body
jokes.explanation: One word doing maximum work. 'Boom!' as Dennis's response to any opportunity to show his body is perfect character economy. The visual of Dennis immediately posing is implied and funny.

jokes.text: You're nothing without Green Man.
jokes.setup: Dee insists no more Green Man in the videos
jokes.punchline: Charlie's parting shot — delivered as a sincere artistic judgment — is funny because he genuinely believes it
jokes.explanation: Perfect Charlie logic and delivery. 'You're nothing without Green Man' has the structure of a serious artistic assessment — the juxtaposition of gravitas and subject matter is the joke. Very quotable in context.

jokes.text: Hey, diary. It's me. It's Thursday, September 30th about midnight. I'm alone, of course, again. And I just had a little bit too much ice cream.
jokes.setup: We cut to what appears to be a private video diary — a new 'character'
jokes.punchline: Dee is performing 'PatheticGirl43' — a lonely, over-sharing internet diarist — with the specific detail of too much ice cream as the saddest possible midnight activity
jokes.explanation: The specific details — midnight, Thursday, 'a little bit too much ice cream' — make this feel genuinely observed. It's cringe but oddly poignant. The joke later payoffs when it turns out this got 80k views, suggesting real audiences find this relatable. 'Of course, again' is a great small touch.

jokes.text: "Interesting." (Charlie's reaction to watching the PatheticGirl43 video)
jokes.setup: Charlie watches Dee perform the lonely midnight diary entry
jokes.punchline: His single word reaction — 'Interesting' — delivered while watching something deeply sad and strange, implies a calculating mind recognizing content potential
jokes.explanation: One word carrying the entire joke. 'Interesting' implies Charlie sees viral potential in Dee's pathetic suffering — which is confirmed when it gets 80k views. Perfect economy. The audience knows something Dee doesn't.

jokes.text: Mac wants to find his 'true love' among the models using The Bachelor format: 'You get a whole bunch of them together, you make them compete over you, bing-bang-boom, soulmate.'
jokes.setup: Mac pulls Frank aside to tell him he's changed his mind about the contest — he wants to find true love
jokes.punchline: Mac's sincere plan to find a soulmate using Bachelor mechanics ('bing-bang-boom, soulmate') reveals a romantic who is also a complete idiot
jokes.explanation: 'Bing-bang-boom, soulmate' is a great compression of The Bachelor premise into something that sounds more like a business deal. Mac's combination of sentimentality and pragmatism is good character work.

jokes.text: Mac spontaneously gives Dennis all the female contestants: 'You take the girls, and I'll take Dennis and the dudes.'
jokes.setup: Mac is interviewing female models as potential soulmates
jokes.punchline: Mac's arrangement — offering Dennis the women and keeping the men for himself — is presented as generous but reads as very revealing about Mac's preferences
jokes.explanation: One of the show's consistent long-form jokes about Mac's closeted homosexuality — this moment is a perfect expression of it, done through implication rather than statement. Mac genuinely thinks he's being generous while revealing exactly who he wants to spend time with. The character integration is superb.

jokes.text: Today's theme is barnyard. Here's a baby pool that you're all going to get into. And there's hay and there's some chickens and ducks.
jokes.setup: Mac announces the theme for the male model competition
jokes.punchline: 'Barnyard' as a male model theme, complete with baby pool, real animals, and hay — there is no connection to a pub billboard and Mac provides no explanation
jokes.explanation: The barnyard theme escalates the absurdity of the whole competition beautifully. The specificity of a 'baby pool' rather than a full pool is a great detail — it's pathetic AND disgusting.

jokes.text: What the hell, bro? Is this supposed to be dirt? It smells like shit. / It is shit. This is a barnyard.
jokes.setup: Models step into the barnyard set and encounter what they think might be mud
jokes.punchline: Mac confirms it's actual shit — real barnyard animal feces — delivered as an obvious clarification, as if real shit is a natural production choice
jokes.explanation: The deadpan delivery of 'It is shit. This is a barnyard.' is excellent. Mac's logic — barnyards have shit, we made a barnyard, therefore: shit — is impeccable absurdist reasoning. Great structure: question, denial, confirmation, explanation.

jokes.text: No one is going to step in shit. / Rex, are you kidding me? Seriously, are you just gonna step right in it? / I want to win, bro. Billboard.
jokes.setup: Mac reveals the set is covered in real manure; models refuse to step in it
jokes.punchline: Rex — without hesitation — steps directly into the shit, motivated by the glory of a free billboard appearance
jokes.explanation: 'I want to win, bro. Billboard.' is a perfect two-sentence motivation. Rex's immediate, confident shit-stepping for the prize of an unpaid billboard appearance is a great absurdist character beat. The 'bro. Billboard.' rhythm is punchy and memorable. Mac's stunned reaction is the button.

jokes.text: This is Taiwan Tammy. She on runway and do a drag queen in nails.
jokes.setup: Dee appears in a new character costume and Charlie asks what she's doing
jokes.punchline: Taiwan Tammy is yet another ethnic stereotype — Dee's confidence in describing a character defined entirely by broken English and drag queen nails is the cringe
jokes.explanation: Taiwan Tammy is a weaker joke than Martina Martinez — the concept is thinner and the execution more reliant on cheap ethnic stereotype. The 'Are you kidding me? That is extremely racist' acknowledgment from Charlie redeems it slightly as self-aware, but the joke itself isn't strong.

jokes.text: Dee as Taiwan Tammy: 'She on runway and do a drag queen in nails.'
jokes.setup: Dee unveils yet another character
jokes.punchline: Taiwan Tammy is an Asian drag queen character described with the same enthusiasm as Martina Martinez — it's the same joke, just more layers of racism
jokes.explanation: It's a repeated beat — Dee with another offensive character. The diminishing returns are intentional (showing Dee won't stop) but it's weaker than the first iteration. 'She on runway and do a drag queen in nails' as a character description is at least specific in its wrongness.

jokes.text: Isn't it awesome? I'm so excited about this one.
jokes.setup: Charlie (correctly) points out Taiwan Tammy is extremely racist
jokes.punchline: Dee's response is pure enthusiasm — she has completely absorbed the critique and discarded it instantly
jokes.explanation: Dee's moral obliviousness is a consistent source of comedy. The gap between 'that's extremely racist' and 'isn't it awesome?' needs no bridge — Dee provides none. Good economy.

jokes.text: Why are your hands in your pockets? / They're itchy. / Your hands are itchy? / Your hands are in your pockets 'cause they're itchy?
jokes.setup: Dee notices Charlie has his hands conspicuously in his pockets
jokes.punchline: Charlie's explanation — 'they're itchy' — is so unsatisfying that Dee repeats it back twice in disbelief; the audience knows the Green Man suit is under there
jokes.explanation: The repetition of 'your hands are itchy' three times with increasing disbelief is a good structural beat. The audience is ahead of Dee — we know the Green Man is coming — which adds anticipation. Good misdirection setup.

jokes.text: Goddamn it! I knew it! Charlie, what are you doing? I said no Green Man! / Green Man sells this whole thing. / It doesn't make any sense! Goddamn it, Charlie!
jokes.setup: Charlie's itchy hands revealed to be Green Man suit
jokes.punchline: Green Man appears despite Dee's explicit prohibition — Charlie's 'Green Man sells this whole thing' is delivered as obvious wisdom
jokes.explanation: The Green Man running gag pays off here with the reveal. The structure — Charlie signals it, Dee confronts it, Green Man appears anyway — is well-executed. 'Green Man sells this whole thing' as Charlie's sincere artistic justification is funny. Third instance of this argument.

jokes.text: Hey, I know you. Yeah, you that girl, PatheticGirl43. I almost didn't recognize you in that getup, but I recognize that whiny voice anywhere.
jokes.setup: A random person recognizes Dee from the internet
jokes.punchline: The recognition comes not from her acting work but from her leaked pathetic video diary — and the person recognizes her 'whiny voice'
jokes.explanation: Perfect irony. Dee gets famous but for exactly the wrong reason — her genuine pathetic suffering rather than her 'characters.' The 'whiny voice' detail is specific and cutting. The payoff to the PatheticGirl43 setup is structurally satisfying.

jokes.text: In other news, it seems like I have a rash in a place where a sexually active person should have a rash.
jokes.setup: We're watching the PatheticGirl43 video diary
jokes.punchline: Dee's clinical overshare — 'in a place where a sexually active person should have a rash' — is both a TMI moment and a weird flex; she's framing an STI symptom as evidence of sexual activity
jokes.explanation: One of the best lines in the episode. The phrasing 'a place where a sexually active person should have a rash' is brilliantly constructed — the qualifier 'should' implies she's proud of the rash as a sign of a sex life, while simultaneously oversharing an STI to a camera. Perfectly captures the PatheticGirl persona. High quotability.

jokes.text: Oh, my God, you put that on YouTube? / Oh, my God, I totally did. / Charlie, why would you do that to me? / Because that's great stuff. / That was my private video diary. / 80,000 hits.
jokes.setup: Dee realizes she's been recognized as PatheticGirl43
jokes.punchline: Charlie reveals he uploaded her private diary without permission; his defense — '80,000 hits' — treats view count as complete moral justification
jokes.explanation: Charlie's moral calculus — 80,000 views = ethical — is both absurd and weirdly prophetic of internet culture. The escalating violation (private diary → public internet) and Charlie's breezy non-apology is great character work. 'That was my private video diary / 80,000 hits' is a perfect two-line joke structure.

jokes.text: You know what it's like for Chocolate Rain when he goes around in the world? He gets free food. He gets free everything because people love that guy.
jokes.setup: Charlie tries to convince Dee to embrace being PatheticGirl43
jokes.punchline: Charlie's reference to 'Chocolate Rain' (a 2007 viral sensation) as a model of internet fame — with the specific detail that he 'gets free food' — is both culturally specific and charmingly naive about how internet fame works
jokes.explanation: Specific 2007 cultural reference adds texture. 'He gets free food' is a funny reduction of internet fame's benefits to the most basic perk. Charlie's sincere admiration for Chocolate Rain is in character. Ages somewhat given the reference is now dated.

jokes.text: Okay, Anya, so they are in fact, double Ds. / That's great news.
jokes.setup: Mac is interviewing female contestants; apparently he had a question about breast size
jokes.punchline: 'That's great news' treats the confirmation of cup size with the gravity of a business report — Mac's formal professionalism applied to objectification
jokes.explanation: 'That's great news' as a response to breast size confirmation is a funny piece of deadpan. Mac's professional interviewer persona applied to an absurd context is consistent character comedy.

jokes.text: Let me ask you a question though. Why should I pick you over the other girls? / I'm willing to do anything in order to win. / You're talking about banging me, right? / Maybe. / If you say yes... / Yes. / Okay, great. You said yes. That's written down now. That's like a contract. All right, perfect. Can't go back on it.
jokes.setup: Mac's official-sounding interview question receives an open-ended answer
jokes.punchline: Mac immediately interprets 'willing to do anything' as a sexual offer, confirms it, then treats verbal consent as a binding legal contract he documents
jokes.explanation: The 'that's like a contract' beat is the best part — Mac's legal framing of an informal verbal exchange is funny and character-appropriate (the gang always believes their internal rules constitute law). The sequence is a bit long but the payoff is good.

jokes.text: I feel like there's vibing happening right now. / Yeah. / I feel like we're completing each other's... / ...sentences. / Yeah, I was gonna say sentences! / I know. / Oh, my God! / How did you read my...? / ...mind? / I was gonna say 'head,' but that's okay, all right. We got, we're one for two.
jokes.setup: Mac is trying to build a romantic connection with Rochelle through sentence completion
jokes.punchline: They complete one sentence correctly (sentences) but Mac was going to say 'head' — which both completes the sentence differently and has an obvious crude meaning — his '50%/one for two' assessment is businesslike
jokes.explanation: Well-structured comedic sequence. The sentence completion game is a known romantic trope; getting it wrong once and scoring it '50%, one for two' is funny deflation. The double meaning of 'head' is delivered naturally rather than forced. Mac's business-like assessment of their romantic compatibility is good character work.

jokes.text: Rex, that is a sexy jaguar. I mean, that jaguar is fierce! I've never been turned on by a jaguar before. This has totally changed my mind toward jaguars.
jokes.setup: Rex is posing in the barnyard theme, apparently dressed as or embodying a jaguar
jokes.punchline: Mac's escalating sexual enthusiasm for Rex-as-jaguar — 'I've never been turned on by a jaguar before' — is an accidental admission wrapped in animal metaphor
jokes.explanation: One of the best jokes in the episode. Mac's closeted sexuality expressed through enthusiasm for Rex's animal pose is pitch-perfect. 'This has totally changed my mind toward jaguars' is an absurd escalation that works because it's simultaneously about jaguars AND about Mac's feelings about men. The specificity of 'jaguars' and 'my mind toward jaguars' is hilarious. High quotability.

jokes.text: Dennis, your mule is shit. / I'm no longer turned on by mules.
jokes.setup: Mac has just declared Rex's jaguar pose sexy; Dennis has apparently posed with a mule
jokes.punchline: Frank's blunt 'your mule is shit' followed by Mac's 'I'm no longer turned on by mules' — a callback to his jaguar enthusiasm — perfectly deflates Dennis
jokes.explanation: Excellent callback execution. 'I'm no longer turned on by mules' works as a direct structural parallel to the jaguar line — by using the same format, the joke pays off both the previous moment AND Dennis's failure simultaneously. 'Your mule is shit' is a great Frank line. Very high quotability. Economy is superb.

jokes.text: Dennis, your mule is shit. / I'm no longer turned on by mules.
jokes.setup: Dennis has apparently chosen a mule as his barnyard animal
jokes.punchline: Frank's double dismissal — 'your mule is shit' (performance critique) followed immediately by 'I'm no longer turned on by mules' (personal sexual reassessment) — is delivered as one continuous judgment
jokes.explanation: Perfect callback and contrast to the jaguar moment — 'I'm no longer turned on by mules' implies Frank was previously turned on by mules, which is both funny on its own and sets up a running implication about Frank's relationship with livestock. The economy is excellent — both sentences are short, devastating, and perfectly paired.

jokes.text: You gave Rex jaguar! There aren't jaguars in barns. What the hell am I supposed to do with a mule? You can't make a mule sexy.
jokes.setup: Dennis realizes Rex was given a jaguar while he got a mule
jokes.punchline: Dennis's protest correctly notes that Rex got a cooler animal — his logic 'you can't make a mule sexy' is both true and an absurd complaint to have
jokes.explanation: 'You can't make a mule sexy' is a great line — it's both obviously true and an absurd thing to need to defend. Dennis's barnyard-accuracy argument ('there aren't jaguars in barns') is funny because he thinks fairness is the issue, not that the whole premise is insane.

jokes.text: Jesus Christ, Frank. I got burns! What are you doing? / Anything can happen on a runway, Dennis. / Nobody's gonna throw detergent in my eyeballs on a runway, Frank!
jokes.setup: Frank is running some kind of runway event; Dennis appears to have had detergent thrown in his eyes
jokes.punchline: Frank's 'anything can happen on a runway' as justification for chemical eye burns, and Dennis's correction — nobody does that on runways — is a perfect absurdist exchange
jokes.explanation: Frank's runway sabotage logic — 'anything can happen' applied to chemical burns — is great absurdist escalation. Dennis's straight-man correction is funny precisely because he's right: no, that doesn't happen on runways. The specificity of 'detergent in my eyeballs' elevates it above a generic sabotage joke.

jokes.text: Check out this tasty delight. You got to eat cockroaches next. / You know what, man? Screw this. I'm outta here. Finished. / Jesus, Rex, I didn't tell you to start eating yet. / That doesn't disqualify me, does it? / No, you're good.
jokes.setup: Frank reveals the next competition event: eating cockroaches
jokes.punchline: Dennis quits; Rex has already started eating before being told to — his dedication to the competition is so pure he pre-ate cockroaches — and Mac's 'No, you're good' treats this as a procedural question
jokes.explanation: Rex eating cockroaches unprompted, then asking if that disqualifies him, is one of the episode's best moments. 'No, you're good' as Mac's instant ruling is perfect — no hesitation, no moral concern, just competition protocol. Rex's pure dedication to winning an unpaid billboard is a great recurring character joke. The structure (Dennis quits → Rex already eating → procedural question) is tight.

jokes.text: Listen, today was the worst day ever. I had an audition, and I didn't get the part, which is really, really strange for me. But then the casting director called, and they were, like, 'We thought you were just better for a different part.' And I was, like, 'That makes more sense.'
jokes.setup: We cut to another PatheticGirl43 diary entry
jokes.punchline: Dee's narcissistic interpretation of rejection as redirection — 'that makes more sense' — reveals the delusion that the casting director's consolation call was genuine
jokes.explanation: 'That makes more sense' as Dee's response to a standard rejection consolation is perfectly delusional. She fully accepts that she's 'better for a different part' — the audience knows the casting director was just being polite. High character integration because this is exactly Dee's pattern of turning failures into victories in her own mind.

jokes.text: Are you guys shooting a porn? / No, we're not... / Never mind. I don't care.
jokes.setup: Dennis walks in on Dee in elaborate character makeup with Charlie filming
jokes.punchline: Dennis's first read of the situation is that it's pornography — and he immediately stops caring when corrected
jokes.explanation: 'Never mind. I don't care.' is a great button — Dennis dismisses the entire scene once his interest (porn) is not present. Good economy. Standard IASIP beat but executed cleanly.

jokes.text: Dude, I realized something. I don't need validation anymore. How great is that? But what I do need is I need the company credit card so that I can buy myself a billboard, get myself out there and show the entire world that Dennis Reynolds still has a rocking body that deserves to be worshipped.
jokes.setup: Dennis tells Charlie and Dee he's moved past needing external validation
jokes.punchline: His 'I don't need validation' is immediately followed by the most validation-seeking plan imaginable — buying a personal billboard to announce his body to the world
jokes.explanation: One of the strongest jokes in the episode. The structure is perfect: assertion of self-sufficiency → immediate total contradiction. 'A rocking body that deserves to be worshipped' is peak Dennis language — 'deserves to be worshipped' frames his physique as a gift to humanity. The character integration is near-perfect; this could only be Dennis Reynolds.

jokes.text: Hey, everybody, PatheticGirl43 here coming to you live with Philadelphia's next hot model Dennis Reynolds. Dennis, tell us what it's like to be so handsome. / Well, I like to think I've been this handsome since birth, possibly even earlier.
jokes.setup: Charlie's plan: Dee interviews Dennis as PatheticGirl43, mixing both their ridiculous agendas
jokes.punchline: 'Possibly even earlier' — Dennis claims to have been handsome before birth, in utero, which is both biologically confused and gloriously specific narcissism
jokes.explanation: 'Possibly even earlier' is a great line — the add-on that extends handsomeness past birth into prenatal existence is perfectly Dennis. The escalation from 'since birth' (already strange) to 'possibly even earlier' (impossible and funnier) is excellent structure. High quotability because it's unexpected and very specific to Dennis's character.

jokes.text: Hey, everybody, PatheticGirl43 here coming to you live with Philadelphia's next hot model Dennis Reynolds. Dennis, tell us what it's like to be so handsome. / Well, I like to think I've been this handsome since birth, possibly even earlier.
jokes.setup: Dee and Charlie have incorporated Dennis into their YouTube scheme
jokes.punchline: Dennis's answer to 'what's it like to be handsome' is that he's been handsome 'since birth, possibly even earlier' — the 'possibly even earlier' extending his handsomeness to the womb (or beyond) is perfect narcissistic absurdism
jokes.explanation: One of the best Dennis lines in the episode. 'Since birth, possibly even earlier' is a perfect construction — it starts with a joke (of course you're born looking a certain way) and then escalates to the absurd (even earlier than birth implies pre-natal or soul-level handsomeness). It's short, perfectly constructed, and completely Dennis. Very quotable. The callback Green Man interruption immediately following makes the setup even funnier in context.

jokes.text: Green Man appears suddenly behind Dennis during the interview, interrupting the shot.
jokes.setup: Dee and Dennis are doing their joint PatheticGirl43/Dennis interview
jokes.punchline: Green Man crashes the frame one more time — the third iteration of this running gag, now completely expected but executed with fresh energy
jokes.explanation: Third iteration of the Green Man gag. By now the audience expects it, which creates anticipation rather than surprise. The timing — right after Dennis's beautiful 'possibly even earlier' line — is good. Running gags improve on rewatch. Structurally solid if not groundbreaking.

jokes.text: This shamrock... will be awarded to the winner as a symbol of my vote and love for this competion.
jokes.setup: Mac is presiding over the female model finale with an awards ceremony
jokes.punchline: The prize is a shamrock — a cheap bar decoration — which Mac presents as a formal symbol of 'vote and love'; the word 'love' is especially funny given the competition context
jokes.explanation: The shamrock as a prize is a funny prop detail — it's completely worthless, clearly grabbed from behind a bar somewhere. Mac's ceremonial gravity is consistent character work. Functional but not standout.

jokes.text: Mac's Bachelor finale: gives shamrock to Rochelle for teaching him 'love, respect, inner beauty' — then produces a second shamrock and gives it to Dominique for banging him, plus Tabitha for doing the same, and 'most importantly, you banged each other, and you let me watch.'
jokes.setup: Mac is running his Bachelor finale, delivering emotional speeches about what each woman taught him
jokes.punchline: After a sincere speech about inner beauty, Mac reveals he had a second shamrock all along and gives it to the women who slept with him — with the highest praise reserved for the ones 'who banged each other and let me watch'
jokes.explanation: The structure here is excellent — Mac builds genuine romantic tension with the inner beauty speech, then completely subverts it with the second shamrock reveal and the escalating 'banged me / banged each other / let me watch' hierarchy. 'I had two of them. I tricked you.' is a great delivery. The escalation from the sincere to the squalid is well-paced.

jokes.text: Rochelle, you taught me about love, respect, inner beauty. / ... / Dominique, you banged me, like, right away. I hardly had to do anything. Tabitha, you did the same. / But most importantly, you banged each other. / And you let me watch.
jokes.setup: Mac delivers his elimination speech, weighing contestants' merits
jokes.punchline: The escalation from romantic virtues (love, respect) to sexual transactions to 'you banged each other and let me watch' reveals that all of Mac's 'soul mate' talk was entirely transactional
jokes.explanation: Excellent escalation structure. The speech begins in the language of a Bachelor elimination ceremony — 'you taught me about love, respect, inner beauty' — before sliding into 'you banged me right away' and ending at 'you banged each other and let me watch.' The 'most importantly' before the voyeurism detail is a perfect rhetorical inversion. Mac has secretly been running The Bachelor for sex tourism the whole episode.

jokes.text: A top of the morning to both of you! / What? / I had two of them. I had another one here. I tricked you.
jokes.setup: Mac is about to give the shamrock to one person
jokes.punchline: He pulls out a second shamrock — he had two the whole time — and gives them to both finalists, revealing 'I tricked you' as the punchline to a trick with no apparent motive
jokes.explanation: 'I tricked you' as a self-satisfied declaration about a trick that benefits everyone (double shamrocks) is very Mac. He loves the idea of being clever even when the trick has no victims. The build — fake-out of awarding just one — and reveal is structurally clean.

jokes.text: But you just said that I taught you about inner beauty and respect. / Yeah, but this whole thing's about banging, and you didn't bang me, so...
jokes.setup: Rochelle protests that Mac gave her the inner-beauty speech but is now excluding her
jokes.punchline: Mac's 'yeah, but this whole thing's about banging' is the most honest statement in the episode — he drops all Bachelor pretense in one sentence
jokes.explanation: Mac cutting directly to 'this whole thing's about banging' after the elaborate Bachelor setup is a great comedic reversal. The trailing 'so...' is a perfect non-conclusion — he has nothing else to add.

jokes.text: But you just said that I taught you about inner beauty and respect. / Yeah, but this whole thing's about banging, and you didn't bang me, so...
jokes.setup: Rochelle objects that Mac just praised her for inner beauty
jokes.punchline: Mac's honest clarification — 'this whole thing's about banging and you didn't bang me' — casually abandons every romantic sentiment he expressed
jokes.explanation: Perfect punctuation on the elimination speech. 'So...' as a trailing acknowledgment — Mac can't even be bothered to finish the sentence explaining why she lost — is good economy. Rochelle's completely valid objection being brushed aside this casually is very funny.

jokes.text: - You're a dick! - I know. And that's what I learned.
jokes.setup: Rochelle calls Mac a dick for his behavior
jokes.punchline: Mac's 'I know. And that's what I learned.' treats the insult as a valuable life lesson from the competition — framing the whole Bachelor parody as a self-discovery exercise
jokes.explanation: Excellent button on the whole Mac subplot. 'And that's what I learned' frames the Bachelor competition as a journey of self-discovery — the lesson being that Mac is, in fact, a dick. His complete peace with this conclusion is perfect character comedy. High economy — five words close the entire arc.

jokes.text: It's a YouTube video that me, Dee and Charlie just made that's gonna get a million hits. So guess what, pal. Don't need your billboard. I'm going viral.
jokes.setup: Dennis confronts Frank about the billboard
jokes.punchline: Dennis confidently declares he's going viral — having just appeared as a vain narcissist in a PatheticGirl43 video interrupted by Green Man — his certainty is completely unwarranted
jokes.explanation: Dennis's misplaced confidence is in character. The irony of 'I'm going viral' applied to whatever that video was is good, though the joke doesn't quite land as sharply as it could — the audience doesn't get to see what's actually in the video.

jokes.text: It's a YouTube video that me, Dee and Charlie just made that's gonna get a million hits. So guess what, pal. Don't need your billboard. I'm going viral.
jokes.setup: Dennis confronts Frank about the billboard
jokes.punchline: Dennis has pivoted from desperately wanting the billboard to declaring he doesn't need it — framing the pivot as a triumph rather than a concession, with 'I'm going viral' as the climactic declaration
jokes.explanation: Dennis's pivot is good character work — his ability to reframe defeat as victory is classic. 'I'm going viral' as the declaration is a period-specific but effective line.

jokes.text: I'm glad you don't need it because you can't have it because it's already up. / What? / Yeah, I put it up right after you called me ugly.
jokes.setup: Dennis tells Frank he doesn't need the billboard; Frank reveals the billboard is already up
jokes.punchline: Frank put the billboard up immediately after being called ugly — his entire motivation was petty revenge, not business
jokes.explanation: Good callback to the opening argument. Frank's pettiness as his primary business motivation is perfectly in character — 'I put it up right after you called me ugly' reveals the whole episode's business rationale was really just wounded pride. Good structural payoff to the opening.

jokes.text: Oh, yeah, sorry about that, Rex. My bad. / So wait. If you already put the billboard up, what'd you put on it?
jokes.setup: Frank reveals the billboard is already up — meaning Rex went through all the shit/cockroaches/etc. for nothing
jokes.punchline: Mac's casual apology to Rex for the entire competition being unnecessary, and Dennis's question setting up the final reveal — 'what did you put on it?'
jokes.explanation: 'Sorry about that, Rex. My bad.' is a perfect one-line dismissal of Rex's entire degrading competition journey. The casualness of the apology for shit-walking and cockroach-eating is very Mac. Sets up the final punchline well.

jokes.text: So wait. If you already put the billboard up, what'd you put on it?
jokes.setup: Frank has revealed the billboard is already up with no explanation of what's on it
jokes.punchline: Mac asks the logical follow-up question — setting up the final joke of the episode (what IS on the billboard?) — the answer is implied to be Frank himself or something equally embarrassing
jokes.explanation: This line functions as the final setup of the episode — the punchline (the actual billboard) is left to audience imagination or presumably a visual reveal. The question itself is well-timed and the implied answer (Frank with two women, thumbs up, as he originally described) would be a perfect callback to his opening vision.

tmdb_overview: Due to the gang's latest "business expenses," Paddy's is in dire need of money. Frank buys a billboard to advertise the bar, but Dee decides to create a viral video to post on YouTube for promotion. Charlie quickly joins her, leaving Frank and Mac to hold a contest for some hot models to feature on the billboard. Naturally, Dennis joins the competition to prove his worth.
